blocks.x: Key definitions

Workbook An Excel file — the container that holds all of your work. A workbook can contain one or more worksheets (grids of cells), chart sheets (a single chart on its own tab), and macro sheets (used to store older-style Excel 4.0 macros).

Worksheet A single grid of rows and columns — a "sheet" — inside a workbook, where data, formulas and formatting live. Every new workbook (Book1) opens with 3 worksheets by default, named Sheet1, Sheet2 and Sheet3, though this default number can be changed in Excel Options.

Save vs. Save As Save updates the same file, at the same location, under the same name. Save As (or F12) creates a new copy of the file — used the first time a workbook is saved, or whenever you want a different name, location or file type.
Consolidate An Excel feature (Data > Consolidate) that combines values from several worksheets or workbooks into one summary range, using a chosen function such as Sum, Average or Count.

File basics
The everyday commands for getting a workbook onto your screen, choosing several at once, unlocking protected files, importing foreign formats, and saving your work safely.
Opening an existing workbook

items: 1File > Open — from the Backstage view, choose a recent file or browse to a folder.
2Keyboard shortcut Ctrl+O — opens the Open dialog directly from any screen in Excel.
3Quick Access Toolbar — if an Open button has been added to the toolbar above the ribbon, a single click opens the dialog.
4Browse — within the Open screen, click Browse to navigate through drives and folders using the standard file-browser dialog.
5Double-click a shortcut — a workbook icon or a shortcut to it (on the desktop, in File Explorer, or a pinned recent file) can be double-clicked to launch Excel and open that file directly.

blocks.x: Selecting several workbooks at once
Shift+click Click the first file name, then hold Shift and click the last file name in the list — selects that file and every file in between (adjacent/contiguous selection).

Ctrl+click Click a file, then hold Ctrl and click additional file names one at a time — selects only the files you actually click, even if they are not next to each other in the list (non-adjacent selection).
Opening protected workbooks
Excel supports two distinct kinds of workbook password protection, and a workbook may use either or both at once:
Password to Open
Required before the workbook will open at all. Without the exact password, the file cannot be viewed.
Password to Modify
The workbook opens (often read-only), but changes cannot be saved back under the same name unless the correct password is supplied.
Case-sensitive entry Excel passwords must be entered exactly as set, including matching upper- and lower-case letters. "Report2024" and "report2024" are treated as different passwords.
Importing files from other programs
Excel can open (import) many non-native file types directly through File > Open, converting their data into a worksheet. Supported types include:

items: ✓Text files — comma- or tab-delimited data imported via the Text Import Wizard.
✓Lotus 1-2-3 worksheet files (an older competing spreadsheet program).
✓Quattro Pro worksheet files (Corel's spreadsheet program).
✓Microsoft Works 2.0 spreadsheet files.
✓dBASE database files.
✓Excel 4.0 charts, macro sheets and workbooks (legacy Excel formats).
✓HTML documents — web pages containing tables can be opened and their tabular data placed into a worksheet.

blocks.x: Save vs. Save As
Save often Best practice is to save every 10–15 minutes while working, so a crash or power loss costs only a few minutes of unsaved edits rather than an entire session's work.
Saving for the first time
Use File > Save As (or press F12). Excel opens the Save As dialog, where you choose a destination folder, type a file name, and (optionally) pick a file type, then click Save.
Saving an already-saved file
Use File > Save, click the Save icon on the Quick Access toolbar, or press Ctrl+S. The file is overwritten in place with no dialog shown, since the name and location are already known.
Key keyboard shortcuts

Ctrl+O — Open a workbook
Ctrl+S — Save the current workbook
F12 — Save As (choose a new name/location/type)
Ctrl+F4 — Close the current workbook
Naming, security & file operations
What makes a valid Excel file name, how to lock down a workbook with passwords and permissions, how to close safely, and how to copy, move or delete files right from the Open dialog.
File naming rules (Windows 7–10)
Length A file name may be up to 255 characters long, including spaces.
Forbidden characters The following characters cannot be used anywhere in a Windows file name: / ? : * ' < > !

Legacy 8.3 naming The old DOS rule limiting names to 8 characters plus a 3-character extension ("8.3 naming") is no longer required on modern Windows. However, if a long file name is transferred to, or opened on, an older system that still enforces 8.3 naming, the name will be automatically truncated.
Protecting a workbook with passwords
Go to File > Info > Protect Workbook to reveal a menu of protection options:

items: 1Always Open Read-Only — prompts anyone opening the file to open it as read-only, reducing accidental edits (not a hard security barrier).
2Encrypt with Password — sets a password that must be entered to open the file at all; the password must then be re-entered to confirm it, and if forgotten, the file cannot be recovered.
3Protect Current Sheet — restricts what changes can be made to the active worksheet (e.g. locking cells from editing) using an optional password.
4Protect Workbook Structure — prevents worksheets from being added, deleted, moved, hidden or renamed, without unlocking the structure with a password.
5Restrict Access — applies Information Rights Management (IRM) permissions so only authorized people can open, edit, print or forward the file.

blocks.x: Setting & confirming a password When you set a password, Excel always asks you to type it a second time to confirm — this guards against a typo locking you out of your own file. As with opening a protected file, the password is case-sensitive.
Closing a workbook

items: 1File > Close — closes the current workbook but leaves Excel open.
2Title bar close button (×) — the X in the top-right corner of the window; closes the workbook (and Excel, if it is the only one open).
3Ctrl+F4 — keyboard shortcut that closes the active workbook.

blocks.x: Unsaved-changes prompt If a workbook has unsaved changes when you try to close it, Excel displays a prompt asking whether to Save, Don't Save, or Cancel — giving you one last chance to keep your edits.
Copying, moving & deleting files from the Open dialog
Copy / Move
In the Open dialog, right-click a file and choose Copy (to duplicate) or Cut (to move). Navigate to the destination folder, right-click an empty area, and choose Paste.
Delete
Right-click a file in the Open dialog and choose Delete. A confirmation prompt appears, and the file is sent to the Recycle Bin rather than being erased immediately.
Working within a workbook
A workbook is only as useful as the sheets inside it — here's how to add, rename and remove them without disturbing the rest of the file.
Inserting worksheets

items: 1Quick-insert button — click the ⊕ (plus) button located at the bottom of the screen, immediately to the right of the last sheet tab, to add a new blank sheet instantly.
2Ribbon method — go to Home > Cells > Insert > Insert Sheet to add a new worksheet before the currently active tab.

3Inserting several sheets at once — hold Shift and click to select several existing sheet tabs (matching the number of new sheets you want), then use Insert Sheet; Excel adds that many new sheets in one action.

blocks.x: Renaming a worksheet
Two ways to rename Right-click the sheet tab and choose Rename, or simply double-click directly on the sheet's tab name. Either way, the tab name becomes editable — type the new name and press Enter.
Deleting a worksheet

items: 1Ribbon method — select the sheet, then go to Home > Cells > Delete > Delete Sheet.
2Right-click method — right-click the sheet's tab and choose Delete from the shortcut menu.

blocks.x: Caution Deleting a worksheet that contains data is immediate and cannot be undone with Ctrl+Z once other actions follow — Excel will warn you if the sheet contains data before it is removed.
Combining several sheets
Data > Consolidate lets you pull matching figures from several worksheets — or even several workbooks — into one summary table, without manually retyping totals.

Consolidate
A command that combines values from multiple ranges (usually on separate worksheets, but possibly separate workbooks) into a single destination range, applying a summary function such as Sum, Average, Count, Max or Min.
Step-by-step: running a consolidation

items: 1Select the destination range — click the upper-left cell (or select the full range) on the worksheet where the combined summary should appear.
2Open Data > Consolidate — this opens the Consolidate dialog box.
3Choose the Function — pick a summary function from the dropdown, e.g. Sum (most common), Average, Count, Max, Min, and so on.

4Use the Reference box — click inside the Reference text box, then either type a range reference or click the Collapse dialog button to shrink the dialog, select the range directly on the worksheet, and click Expand dialog (or press the button again) to return.
5Click Add — adds the selected reference to the All References list. Repeat steps 4–5 for every worksheet range you want included.
6Set Top Row / Left Column options — check these boxes if the source ranges include row/column headings you want Excel to match by name rather than by plain position.

7Decide on links — check "Create links to source data" if you want the consolidated values to update automatically whenever the source data changes; leave it unchecked to insert fixed values that will not update.
8Click OK — Excel builds the consolidated summary in the destination range.

blocks.x: Consolidating by position vs. by category
By Position
Excel combines values based on where they sit in each source range (e.g. cell B2 on every sheet). This requires every source worksheet to be laid out identically, in the same row/column order.
By Category (Heading)
With Top Row and/or Left Column checked, Excel matches values by their row or column labels instead of their position — useful when sheets list the same categories in a different order.

Fixed values vs. linked values Fixed values (links unchecked) are a one-time snapshot — editing the source sheets later will not update the summary. Linked values (links checked) insert formulas that reference the source ranges, so the summary refreshes automatically whenever the source data changes.
Select Destination→ Data > Consolidate→ Add References→ Choose Function→ OK
